text.en: Athithi Devo Bhava means that a guest is like a god. We welcome guests warmly, listen to them and say kind things. But what if you say exactly the wrong thing every time you open your mouth? That is what happens to Mary in this funny play by G. C. Thornley.

You discuss what Athithi Devo Bhava means and why it is important to be polite to guests. From a list, polite behaviour includes offering water, enquiring about their well-being and accompanying them to the door. Asking when they will leave and criticising their habits are rude. You also think of at least three ways to handle friends who are rude when they disagree, such as listening, staying calm and using polite words.
Mary Shaw is a young girl. Mrs. Shaw is her mother. Mrs. Harding is the wife of a wealthy man, Mr. Harding, and Mrs. Lee is Mr. Harding's married sister. This is a humorous play, in which Mary forgets her mother's advice and commits blunders, which means careless mistakes, and embarrasses the guests and her mother.
Mrs. Shaw tells Mary to put her clothes away because two ladies will soon arrive, and Mary protests that she is not a child. Mrs. Harding's husband has just bought a big house in Lanfield, and they lived in London earlier. Mrs. Shaw met her in a shop and invited her. Mrs. Lee is staying with them. Mary says she can talk very well and wants to stay. Her mother says she talks too much and may not say the right thing, but allows her to stay if she takes care. She wants Mrs. Harding as a friend, because there is not much to do in Lanfield. The advice is: be kind and say things that will please people, laugh and make them laugh, and if everyone stops talking, say something to start the talk again. Do not make them angry. When guests are ready to leave, do not look glad. Ask them to stay a little longer by saying something like Must you go? Can't you stay? Mary repeats these words so as to remember them, and goes to change her dress.
Mrs. Harding says they like Lanfield, though it is not the same as London. No one speaks, and Mrs. Shaw looks at Mary. Mary praises Mrs. Harding's beautiful children, but Mrs. Harding has no children, and is not pleased. Mrs. Shaw quietly says they must be someone else's. Mary then criticises Mr. Best, who goes by train to London every day and works as a banker. Mrs. Lee says her own brother is a banker, and Mary says she is sorry. She then laughs at Mrs. Best's blue dress with a red coat, which Mrs. Harding says she herself often wears. Mrs. Shaw quickly says she likes that combination. She says she cannot understand women who stay in bed in the morning or who often call the doctor, but Mrs. Harding stays in bed in the morning and Mrs. Lee often goes to the doctor. She calls talkative women boring, but Mrs. Lee's mother is talkative, and she goes red. She says men like Mr. Pomeroy who ride horses and practise shooting are hard to understand, and Mrs. Lee says her brother does the same and moved here for it. The guests say it is getting late and they must go. Mrs. Shaw politely asks them to stay a little longer, and Mary, unable to say the right thing even now, says Oh, must you stay? Can't you go? That is the final blunder.
In the rectification exercise, the correct versions are: Mrs. Harding says they like Lanfield very much even though it is not like London; Mrs. Harding was displeased because she has no children; Mrs. Shaw liked Mrs. Best because she is a nice woman, and the newspaper remark was about bankers; Mrs. Harding herself wears a blue dress with a red coat and Mrs. Shaw says she likes it; and Mary was looking at Mr. Pomeroy on his horse outside the window, not a dog. Mary remembers the words but not the advice. Her mistakes come from speaking before thinking, judging people in front of those who know them, and getting the last line backwards. The play teaches us to think before we speak, to be kind, and to remember that remarks about people can hurt, especially when we do not know who is listening. The humour comes from the repeated pattern. Each time Mary criticises someone, a guest turns out to be related to or similar to that person. Mary's mistakes are comic, though they embarrass her mother.
Drama is written as a script with characters' names, spoken lines and directions in brackets, such as quietly or with a red face. These stage directions tell the actor how to speak and act. Polite phrases include Please stay a little longer and It was very good of you to come. Words in the text include hilariously, meaning in a very funny way, blunders, careless mistakes, and embarrasses, makes uncomfortable. Role play: act out the play in groups, taking care with tone of voice and expressions.

prompt.en: Describe how Mary ignored her mother's advice and what the play teaches.

requiredIdeas.en: Her mother told her to be kind and say pleasing things.
She criticised Mr. Best, Mrs. Best, women in bed, talkative women and Mr. Pomeroy, all connected to the guests.
Finally she said Must you stay? Can't you go?
We should think before we speak and be kind to guests.

commonMisconceptions.en: Mary was very polite to the guests.

points.en: Say the Right Thing is a humorous play by G. C. Thornley.
Mary forgets her mother's advice and makes remark after remark that offends the guests.
Her last words, Must you stay? Can't you go?, are the final blunder.
The play teaches us to think before we speak and to be kind and polite to guests.
A play has characters, dialogue and stage directions.
